vignette:
He is a tall man, his frame still solid from decades of physical work, but his hands tremble slightly as he settles into the chair across from me. He speaks in a low, measured voice, his African accent lilting the English words. He tells me he retired last year after thirty-four years as a bomb disposal technician, but the retirement was not his choice. The memory he carries is not of an explosion, but of a silence.

Twenty-two years ago, he was the lead technician on a team called to a makeshift laboratory in a war-torn region. Intelligence suggested a chemical weapon was being assembled inside. He had dismantled hundreds of bombs-improvised, military, even some with crude biological agents. But this was different. The device was rigged to a timer, and he worked quickly, his protective suit cumbersome in the tropical heat. He remembers the moment the seal on a glass vial cracked. A yellowish vapor curled toward his faceplate. The suit's filter had been compromised, and he inhaled before he could hold his breath. He felt a burning in his throat, a metallic taste. The team evacuated him, and the device was later neutralized remotely. But the damage was done.

For months afterward, he suffered from shortness of breath, skin rashes, and a persistent cough. The doctors told him the exposure was low-level, and he would recover fully. But what they could not measure was what settled in his mind. He returned to work, but the world had changed. Every time he approached an unfamiliar package, every time he heard a hiss or smelled something acrid, his chest would tighten, and his vision would blur at the edges. He began to check his equipment twice, three times. His colleagues noticed his hesitation. He started to avoid certain jobs, asking for reassignments to "simple" tasks-training new recruits, maintaining gear. His supervisor, a man he had served with for years, pulled him aside and told him he seemed "on edge." He shrugged it off.

At home, his wife noticed he no longer slept through the night. He would wake drenched in sweat, describing a recurring dream: he is back in that laboratory, the timer ticking, but he cannot move. The yellow vapor fills the room, and he chokes. He would get up and pace the house, checking the locks on the doors, the seals on the windows. She once found him in the garage, holding a can of paint thinner to his nose, trying to see if the smell triggered the memory. He cannot explain why he did it.

Now, at sixty-two, he is a retired man in a quiet suburban house. But his mind remains on high alert. He avoids the garden shed because the smell of old fertilizer reminds him of something he cannot name. He watches the news obsessively, looking for reports of chemical attacks, then changes the channel when they come on. His wife wants to travel, but he refuses to fly-not because of planes, but because he read about an in-flight chemical leak once. He spends most of his time in his workshop, methodically cleaning and organizing tools, as if preparing for a mission that will never come. He tells me that his body is fine now, but his head is not. He says, "I am still in that room. The timer is still ticking."
